books.section: America Transformed into the Industrial Giant of the World (1870–1910)
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Emory R. Johnson, American Railway Transportation (1908), Interstate Commerce Commission railroad mileage; Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), Table IX, steel output

stimulus.text:
The table shows two measures of American industrial growth, 1870-1900.

| Year | Miles of railroad in operation | Steel produced (millions of tons) |
| 1870 | 52,922 | 0.07 |
| 1880 | 93,296 | 1.25 |
| 1890 | 163,597 | 4.28 |
| 1900 | 193,346 | 10.19 |
stimulus.source_note: Railroad mileage from Emory R. Johnson, American Railway Transportation (1908), using Interstate Commerce Commission figures; steel output from the Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), Table IX. The lesson script gives the same scale in round numbers: about 35,000 miles of track in 1865 and over 190,000 by 1900.

stem: Which of the following is the best example of a limitation of the table as evidence about the period?

options.text: It covers too short a span to show any change
options.misconception: Thirty years is enough for both series to grow several times over.

options.text: It proves that industrial growth raised every worker’s wages
options.misconception: Output figures say nothing about wages, so the table cannot prove that.

options.text: It shows how much was produced, but not who gained
It shows that railroads caused the growth of steel
options.misconception: Parallel growth in a table is not proof that one caused the other.

rationales.A: Thirty years shows very large change in both columns.
rationales.B: The table has no wage figures, so it cannot prove anything about wages.
rationales.C: Production totals say nothing about how the gains were shared.
rationales.D: Two series rising together does not prove that one caused the other.
rationales.general:
Ask what the numbers leave out.
1. The table counts miles of track and tons of steel.
2. Counts of output say nothing about wages, prices, or who owned the mills.
3. A table that measures size cannot measure sharing.
4. Background from the books: owners grew rich while many workers stayed poor.
Remember: ask what a source counts, then ask what it cannot count.
